data.title: Trusted Cloud Services Used as a Command Channel
data.summary:
Command and control was conducted through a mainstream cloud service that the
organisation permits and relies upon, so the channel carried the service's own
reputation and could not be blocked without business impact.
data.description:
Using a service the organisation cannot block is the strongest position an operator can
hold. Traffic goes to a provider on every allow-list, with a valid certificate for a
genuine domain, and blocking the destination breaks legitimate work.

This defeats controls built on destination identity, which is most of them. What remains
is the distinction between the organisation's own tenant and an arbitrary one, and
between normal application behaviour and automation — neither of which is visible without
tenant restriction or API-level logging.

Where the service is also used for file storage, the same channel provides exfiltration,
so the control and data paths collapse into one permitted destination.
data.recommendation:
* Apply tenant restrictions so permitted cloud services may only be used with the
  organisation's own tenant.
* Where the service offers API-level audit logging, ingest it; network-level visibility
  will not distinguish tenants.
* Alert on automation patterns against permitted services — regular polling, machine-like
  intervals — rather than on the destination itself.
data.short_recommendation: Restrict permitted cloud services to the corporate tenant and ingest their audit logs.
